title: UK Bans Disposable BBQs as Wildfire Risk Soars During Heatwave
summary:
As the UK swelters under a prolonged heatwave and drought, the government has taken the unusual step of banning the sale of disposable barbecues. The temporary ban, announced Friday, applies to England, Scotland, and Wales, and comes after the devices were linked to "a number of serious wildfires across the country over the summer months."

The decision follows an emergency Cobra meeting earlier this week in response to record temperatures. Prime Minister Andy Burnham did not mince words: "Britain is a tinderbox right now. Setting a fire in any outdoor setting of any kind is a risk to other people's homes, it's a risk to other people's lives, don't do it, please don't do it."

Data from the National Fire Chiefs Council shows 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, matching last year's record. Fire crews in the West Midlands have been battling multiple blazes for a second consecutive day. Burnham said some of those fires were likely started by disposable barbecues, and he announced plans to commission firefighting planes, similar to those used in Europe and the US.

The ban was implemented under advice from the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, which stated that disposable barbecues "cannot be considered a safe product" under current conditions. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds called it a "common-sense step to protect lives and the environment."

Many large retailers had already voluntarily suspended sales of disposable barbecues under a 2023 framework agreed with fire chiefs and the British Retail Consortium. But the new ban makes it mandatory. David Skaith, the Labour mayor for York and North Yorkshire, has been campaigning for a permanent ban on single-use grills and urged the prime minister to make it so.

For now, the message is clear: no open flames, no disposable BBQs, and extreme caution with cigarettes. The UK is facing a wildfire season unlike any in recent memory.
why_it_matters: Britain's wildfire risk shows how climate-driven weather can turn everyday products into public dangers; temporary bans may become permanent if heatwaves continue, changing how people camp, grill, and use public land. It also raises questions about personal convenience versus collective safety during environmental emergencies.

background_read: Disposable barbecues are single-use grills that can stay hot for hours after use; when placed on dry grass or left in warm rubbish, they can ignite wildfires.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham (the UK leader named in the article) described Britain as a 'tinderbox' during the heatwave, a word that compares the dry landscape to material that can catch fire easily.

The National Fire Chiefs Council (the professional body that represents senior fire officers across the UK) records wildfire incidents and has warned that the country's fire season is lengthening as heatwaves become more frequent.

Cobra meetings (emergency sessions named after the Cabinet Office Briefing Rooms, where top ministers and officials coordinate responses to national crises) are usually reserved for major security or weather emergencies.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (the UK ministry responsible for product safety and business regulation) concluded that disposable barbecues 'cannot be considered a safe product' under drought conditions, while many retailers had already voluntarily suspended sales under a 2023 framework agreed with the British Retail Consortium.

perspectives.description: The ban protects homes, lives, and landscapes during extreme fire conditions. Supporters see it as a common-sense step, especially after disposable barbecues were linked to serious wildfires and fire crews were stretched across the country.

Some people may see the ban as an overreach that restricts summer leisure and camping traditions. Retailers that still sold the grills could also face lost sales, and critics may argue a temporary ban is a blunt tool that does not address careless behavior.

The UK has traditionally had a lower wildfire risk than places like southern Europe or the western United States, but climate change is altering that pattern. Voluntary retailer suspensions were not enough, so the government moved to mandatory action, showing how product bans can follow voluntary failures.

If heatwaves continue, the temporary ban could become permanent, a change David Skaith is already urging. The government is also considering firefighting planes, suggesting the UK may need to rethink both land management and public behavior as wildfire seasons intensify.
